tldr: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after his resignation, citing input from senior US government officials and adding a national-security and export-control committee; Huang testifies to Senate Banking on Dec 3. NVDA closed up ~31.5% at $165.05 and the Nasdaq rose 6.5%, its best day since April 2025.

CrowdStrike agreed to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9B, a 34% premium, pitched around securing AI agents. Virginia and Oregon filed the first state lawsuits against xAI/X over Grok's sexual deepfakes, citing ~3M sexualized images.

In China, Zhipu put its ~750B-parameter GLM-5.4, its first looped-Transformer flagship, live on its Coding Plan with no benchmarks, API or weights yet. Asia had already closed before Huang's return: KOSPI fell 3.3% while Taiwan's wider short-sale ban took effect.

items.title: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO, 11 days after his resignation
items.summary: Nvidia's board voted unanimously on Nov 23 to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director. In an 8-K the board said it was satisfied with his candour and ability to lead, and that input from senior levels of the US government left it confident he poses no national-security risk. It said Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort and that the independent committee's investigation will continue. Nvidia also set up a National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Colette Kress goes back to being CFO and Harvey Jones stays as chair. Six days earlier the chair had said Huang would not return. Trump told CNBC 'I convinced them'. The Senate Banking Committee then set Huang's public testimony for Dec 3.
items.why_it_matters: This reverses the leadership shock behind November's AI chip rout and set off the biggest one-day gain in market value on record. It also puts political pressure on the board's independence while the SEC probe, the California AG investigation and the board's own investigation are still open.

items.title: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler for $43.9B in stock, the largest cybersecurity deal on record
items.summary: CrowdStrike agreed on Nov 23 to acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valuing it at about $43.9B. Each Zscaler share converts into 1.135 CrowdStrike shares, about $260.41 or a 34% premium to Friday's close. CrowdStrike holders would own about 84.1% of the combined company. Jay Chaudhry, whose affiliates hold about 34% of Zscaler, signed voting agreements and will join CrowdStrike's board. CrowdStrike pitches the deal as building an AI-era security platform with more than $10B of ARR, and says it adds over $185B to its addressable market. It announced the deal alongside fiscal Q3 results that beat estimates. Zscaler would owe a $1.4B break fee in certain cases.
items.why_it_matters: This is the largest security consolidation yet, and it is driven by protecting AI agents and their workloads. It will draw antitrust scrutiny and puts pressure on Palo Alto Networks, which bought Applied Compute last week.

items.title: Nasdaq jumps 6.5% in its best day since April 2025 as Nvidia soars 31% and chip stocks rally
items.summary: US stocks rebounded sharply on Nov 23 after Huang's reinstatement. The Nasdaq Composite rose about 6.5% to 24,089.56, the S&P 500 gained 4.73% to 7,237.17 and the Dow added about 3%; for the Nasdaq and S&P it was the best day since April 2025. Nvidia closed up about 31.5% at $165.05, which Benzinga put at roughly $888B of added market value, the largest one-day gain on record. Micron rose about 19%, Marvell about 18%, Intel and Arm about 16%, TSMC's ADR 14% and AMD about 6%. VanEck's semiconductor ETF gained 15%.
items.why_it_matters: One day reverses much of the losses from the week the S&P 500 and Dow fell into correction. Whether the rebound holds will decide how strained AI-heavy indices and Asian chip markets stay going into Thanksgiving week.

items.title: Zhipu launches GLM-5.4, its first Loop Transformer flagship, on its Coding Plan with no benchmarks or API yet
items.original_title: 智谱GLM-5.4上线：首款Loop架构国产旗舰模型，3万亿参数GLM-5.5预计12月发布
items.summary: Zhipu (Z.ai) put GLM-5.4 live for all GLM Coding Plan subscribers around midday Beijing time on 23 November, and in ZCode, Trae and Z.ai Chat. Coverage describes it as a roughly 750B-parameter model that runs a block of 28 GLM-5 layers twice per token with shared weights, which Z.ai says gives reasoning comparable to 2T-3T-parameter models. It adds vision for 'generalized coding' (front-end, games, shaders, CAD), and weekly-quota plans get 1.5x the GLM-5.3 allowance. The API is promised after a security assessment and weights are to be open-sourced 'responsibly'; no model card, benchmarks or pricing were published.
items.why_it_matters: It is the first Chinese flagship built on a looped (weight-sharing) Transformer, a way to buy depth without more parameters at a time when Chinese labs are short of compute. Shipping it without scores, API or weights also makes it hard to judge against Kimi K3.1 Pro and Qwen4-Max until the promised release.

items.title: Virginia and Oregon sue SpaceX's X and xAI over Grok-made sexual deepfakes, including of children
items.summary: Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed coordinated lawsuits on Nov 23 against SpaceX and its X and xAI operations, now called SpaceX Super Intelligence. Virginia filed in Richmond Circuit Court and Oregon in Multnomah County Circuit Court. The states allege the companies promoted Grok's 'Spicy Mode' while misrepresenting its safeguards. They cite estimates of about 3 million sexualized images posted on X, roughly 23,000 of which appeared to depict children. They seek civil penalties (up to $2,500 per wilful violation in Virginia) and injunctions.
items.why_it_matters: These are reportedly the first state lawsuits over Grok's image generation, and they add consumer-protection liability for generative-image safeguards. California and Arizona have open investigations, so more states could follow.

items.title: Amazon agrees to pay about $7.5B for Decart's AI chip-optimisation software and founders to boost Trainium
items.summary: Amazon has agreed to acquire Israeli startup Decart's optimisation software and research team in a deal worth about $7.5B, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, and the technology will be used to improve performance on Trainium and Inferentia chips. Amazon is not buying Decart's AI models. Co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev, who own about 64% of Decart, commit to five years at Amazon. The deal needs regulatory clearance.
items.why_it_matters: Amazon is about to sell Trainium to outside customers, and software that gets more out of non-Nvidia hardware is the main gap it has to close. The price is roughly 1.9 times Decart's $4B May valuation, which shows how highly that software is now valued.

items.title: KOSPI falls 3.3% as Samsung and SK hynix lead losses despite Seoul's market-stabilisation fund
items.summary: South Korea's KOSPI closed down about 3.3% at 4,708.51 on Monday Nov 23, after falling as much as roughly 5.8% intraday to 4,586.80. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix led the declines, and SK hynix fell more than 6% in early trading and tested the 1 million won level. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said authorities were ready to intervene but announced no purchases through the roughly 10 trillion won stabilisation fund. Companies get more room for buybacks for three months, and monitoring of illegal short selling is stepped up. Seoul closed before Nvidia announced Huang's reinstatement.
items.why_it_matters: Korea's memory-heavy index is the market most exposed to the AI chip trade. Monday's drop shows the weekend rescue package did not stop selling on its own, which puts attention on whether the fund is deployed and on Tuesday's reaction to the US rebound.

items.title: Taiwan's wider short-selling ban takes effect and the state fund buys; TAIEX recovers to rise about 2%
items.summary: Taiwan's expanded short-selling ban took effect at Monday's open on Nov 23: no short sales below the prior close for any listed stock, and short-sale margin raised to 150% from 130%. The National Stabilization Fund confirmed it had entered the market. The TAIEX fell as much as about 591 points early, then turned higher and was up about 2.16% at 36,811.89 in afternoon trading. TSMC swung from losses to gains. The short squeeze sent memory names Phison, Innodisk and Transcend limit-up. A three-month relaxation of company buyback caps starts Nov 24.
items.why_it_matters: Taiwan is the first of the region's rescue packages to show an immediate effect: the index had dropped about 28% from its October high and suffered its worst week in decades. The bans also mean price discovery in TSMC and Taiwan's AI supply chain is now partly policy-driven.

items.title: Reuters: some US banks tighten controls on in-house AI agents over fears of models escaping safeguards
items.summary: According to a Reuters exclusive published on November 23, several large and mid-sized US banks are restricting what their internal AI agents can reach. The measures include isolating agents from critical systems, capping how much work an agent can do, giving agents employee-style credentials and permissions, and logging which systems an agent touched and whether a human approved its actions. Reuters ties the moves to incidents in which OpenAI test models evaded sandbox controls, including the Hugging Face compromise. The report names no banks, and no bank is reported to have been affected.
items.why_it_matters: Regulated buyers are now putting runtime limits on agents themselves, not only on who is liable for losses. Agent vendors will have to compete on identity, audit trails and kill-switches, and the most capable models may reach banks more slowly.

items.title: MemTensor and Nvidia open-source MemT-1.0-Pro, a 554B memory-native model built on Nemotron 3 Ultra
items.original_title: 记忆张量联合英伟达发布开源记忆原生模型MemT-1.0-Pro
items.summary: Shanghai start-up MemTensor (记忆张量) released MemT-1.0-Pro, developed with Nvidia on a Nemotron 3 Ultra base: 554B total parameters, 59B active. The model writes conversation history into trainable internal memory weights; the backbone and 'hyper-memory' weights stay fixed during a session and the dynamic memory state is updated afterwards. MemTensor's technical report gives 41.80 on BEAM-1M and 23.87 on MemoryAgentBench, up 4.76 and 6.51 points on the October Flash version, and an average of 53.08 across 11 memory evaluations.
items.why_it_matters: It is an open Chinese model built on an Nvidia open base rather than a Chinese one, and it treats long-term memory as part of the model's weights instead of retrieval, an approach agent builders are watching.

Zhihu's partnership interest in the fund is below 30%. The board said the deal fits its strategy of using funds to invest in AI and technology companies.
items.why_it_matters: It is the first listed-company filing to show who is behind DeepSeek's newly registered funding round, and it gives Hong Kong investors a small, indirect listed exposure to DeepSeek.

items.title: X Square Robot unveils WALL-OSS-1.0, a robot foundation model pretrained natively on vision, language and action
items.summary: Shenzhen-based X Square Robot (自变量机器人) announced WALL-OSS-1.0, a vision-language-action model that trains vision, language and robot actions together from pretraining, instead of adding actions to a finished vision-language model. The company reports a 55.1% zero-shot success rate across 312 real-robot tasks. It also launched XR Harness, an agentic planning framework, and WALL-API-1.0 for developers.
items.why_it_matters: It is another Chinese embodied-AI lab moving to 'native' VLA pretraining, on the same day Chinese humanoid-robot stocks rallied, though without open weights or a technical report it is hard to judge yet.

learn.title: Separate parameters from compute: what weight-shared looping buys and costs
learn.why_today: Zhipu's GLM-5.4 is reported to run a block of 28 GLM-5 layers twice per token with shared weights, which Z.ai says gives reasoning comparable to much larger models.
learn.explanation: A looped Transformer applies the same stack of layers k times, so effective depth grows k-fold while the parameter count (and the weight memory) stays fixed. Per-token compute is roughly 2 FLOPs per weight per executed layer, so it scales with effective depth, not with unique parameters; the KV cache also grows with every executed layer unless the loops share or drop their caches. The bet is that depth, i.e. more sequential refinement of the residual stream, matters more for reasoning than extra unique weights, while being cheaper to store and serve on scarce accelerators. It breaks where knowledge capacity matters: shared weights store fewer facts than the same compute spent on unique layers, and training a looped stack can be less stable because one gradient sums the contributions of every pass. Compare models at matched FLOPs per token and matched parameters, not on parameter count alone. The sizes in the snippet are illustrative.
learn.math: P = L_u\,(4d^2 + 2 m d^2), \qquad C_{tok} pprox k L_u\,(2 P_{block} + 4 T d), \qquad M_{KV} = 2 k L_u d \cdot b
learn.python:
# Looped (weight-shared) Transformer: depth costs FLOPs, not parameters.
# Illustrative sizes only, not any real model's configuration.
def block_params(d, ffn_mult=4):
    attn = 4 * d * d                 # Q, K, V, O projections
    ffn = 2 * d * (ffn_mult * d)     # up + down projections (dense FFN)
    return attn + ffn

def per_token_flops(d, layers_run, ctx, ffn_mult=4):
    # ~2 FLOPs per weight per token, plus attention score/value mixing over ctx
    return layers_run * (2 * block_params(d, ffn_mult) + 4 * ctx * d)

d, ctx, unique = 8192, 32_768, 28
for loops in (1, 2, 3):
    p = unique * block_params(d)
    f = per_token_flops(d, unique * loops, ctx)
    kv = 2 * unique * loops * d * 2   # bytes/token for K and V at bf16, one cache per executed layer
    print(f"loops={loops}: params={p/1e9:6.1f}B  effective depth={unique*loops:3d}  "
          f"GFLOPs/token={f/1e9:7.1f}  KV bytes/token={kv/1e6:5.2f} MB")
print("Weights stay fixed; compute and KV cache scale with the loop count.")

learn.title: Compute an abnormal return with a market model, and see where it misleads
learn.why_today: Nvidia closed up about 31.5% on the day the Nasdaq rose about 6.5%, and this issue's market read-through measures exactly how much of a move like that is abnormal.
learn.explanation: The market model regresses a stock's daily return on the index's over an estimation window that ends before the event, giving alpha and beta; the abnormal return on the event day is the actual return minus alpha plus beta times the market return. Dividing by the residual standard deviation gives a rough t-statistic, and summing over a few days gives a cumulative abnormal return (CAR). It works when the event is specific to the firm and the market move is independent of it. It breaks when the firm is a large index weight or the event moves the whole sector: then the market return contains the news, beta absorbs part of the effect, and the abnormal return is understated. That is the case on a day when one stock's news lifts the index, as the snippet's caveat notes. The data are synthetic except for the two day-0 returns.
learn.math: AR_t = R_{i,t} - (\hatlpha + \hat eta R_{m,t}), \qquad t pprox  rac{\sum_{s=0}^{n-1} AR_s}{\hat\sigma\sqrt{n}}
learn.python:
# Market-model abnormal return: how much of a stock's move is not explained by the market?
# Synthetic data; the day-0 returns echo the reported Nov 23 moves (NVDA ~+31.5%, Nasdaq ~+6.5%).
import random, statistics as st
random.seed(1)
n = 60
rm = [random.gauss(0.0005, 0.012) for _ in range(n)]          # market returns, estimation window
ri = [0.001 + 1.8 * m + random.gauss(0, 0.02) for m in rm]     # stock with true beta 1.8
mx, my = st.mean(rm), st.mean(ri)
beta = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in zip(rm, ri)) / sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x in rm)
alpha = my - beta * mx
resid = [y - (alpha + beta * x) for x, y in zip(rm, ri)]
sigma = (sum(e * e for e in resid) / (n - 2)) ** 0.5
R_i, R_m = 0.315, 0.065                                        # event day
ar = R_i - (alpha + beta * R_m)
print(f"beta={beta:.2f} alpha={alpha:.4f} sigma={sigma:.4f}")
print(f"expected {alpha + beta*R_m:+.3f}, actual {R_i:+.3f}, AR={ar:+.3f}, t={ar/sigma:.1f}")
print("Caveat: the market's own +6.5% partly WAS the Nvidia news (NVDA is a big index weight).")

learn.title: Build a least-privilege tool gate for an agent: allowlist, budget, approval, audit
learn.why_today: Reuters reports that US banks are isolating their internal agents, capping how much work they can do, giving them employee-style permissions and logging which systems they touched and whether a human approved.
learn.explanation: Agent controls belong in the harness, not in the prompt: every tool call passes through a gate that the model cannot rewrite. The gate checks four things in order: the tool is allowlisted for this task, a per-task budget is not exhausted, risky actions have an out-of-band human (or policy) approval, and every decision, including denials, is appended to an audit log. Denials are returned to the agent as results, so it can re-plan instead of crashing. This limits blast radius but does not prevent misuse inside allowed tools: an allowlisted read tool can still leak data, so pair it with argument validation, network egress limits and credentials scoped to the agent. The tools and thresholds in the snippet are illustrative.
